solution:
\(f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 12x - 16\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 12 = 3(x^2 - 4x + 4) = 3(x - 2)^2\)
A perfect square is never negative, so \(f'(x) = 3(x - 2)^2 \ge 0\) for every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), and \(f'(x) = 0\) only at the single isolated point \(x = 2\).
Since \(f'(x) \ge 0\) throughout the domain and vanishes only at one isolated point, the graph never turns.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is an increasing function on \(\mathbb{R}\).

\(f(x) = 2 - 3x + 3x^2 - x^3\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = -3 + 6x - 3x^2 = -3(x^2 - 2x + 1) = -3(x - 1)^2\)
A perfect square is never negative, so \(-3(x - 1)^2 \le 0\) for every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), and \(f'(x) = 0\) only at the single isolated point \(x = 1\).
Since \(f'(x) \le 0\) throughout the domain and vanishes only at one isolated point, the graph never turns.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is a decreasing function on \(\mathbb{R}\).

\(f(x) = x - \dfrac{1}{x}\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(x \neq 0\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 1 + \dfrac{1}{x^2} = \dfrac{x^2 + 1}{x^2}\)
For every \(x \neq 0\), the numerator \(x^2 + 1 > 0\) and the denominator \(x^2 > 0\).
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) at every point of the domain.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is an increasing function wherever it is defined, i.e. it is increasing on \((-\infty, 0)\) and increasing on \((0, \infty)\).
(The domain is broken at \(x = 0\), so the two branches are stated separately; on each branch \(f\) rises steadily.)

\(f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 6\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12 = 6(x^2 - x - 2) = 6(x - 2)(x + 1)\)
\(f\) is strictly increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\), i.e. where \((x - 2)(x + 1) > 0\).
The critical points are \(x = -1\) and \(x = 2\). Testing the sign of \((x - 2)(x + 1)\) in the three intervals:
For \(x < -1\): both factors are negative \(\Rightarrow\) product positive.
For \(-1 < x < 2\): \((x + 1) > 0\), \((x - 2) < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) product negative.
For \(x > 2\): both factors are positive \(\Rightarrow\) product positive.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly increasing for \(x \in (-\infty, -1) \cup (2, \infty)\), i.e. for \(x < -1\) or \(x > 2\).

\(f(x) = 3 + 3x - 3x^2 + x^3\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 3 - 6x + 3x^2 = 3(x^2 - 2x + 1) = 3(x - 1)^2\)
A perfect square is never negative, so \(f'(x) = 3(x - 1)^2 \ge 0\) for every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).
\(f'(x) > 0\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \((x - 1)^2 > 0\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(x \neq 1\).
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) except \(x = 1\), so \(f\) is strictly increasing for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(x \neq 1\) — that is, on \((-\infty, 1)\) and on \((1, \infty)\).
Note: since \(f'\) vanishes only at the single isolated point \(x = 1\) and is positive on both sides of it, the graph does not flatten out over any interval; \(f\) in fact rises steadily across the whole of \(\mathbb{R}\).

\(f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 - 36x + 7\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x - 36 = 3(x^2 - 4x - 12) = 3(x - 6)(x + 2)\)
\(f\) is strictly increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\), i.e. where \((x - 6)(x + 2) > 0\).
The critical points are \(x = -2\) and \(x = 6\). Testing signs:
For \(x < -2\): both factors are negative \(\Rightarrow\) product positive.
For \(-2 < x < 6\): \((x + 2) > 0\), \((x - 6) < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) product negative.
For \(x > 6\): both factors are positive \(\Rightarrow\) product positive.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly increasing for \(x \in (-\infty, -2) \cup (6, \infty)\), i.e. for \(x < -2\) or \(x > 6\).

\(f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 6\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12 = 6(x^2 - x - 2) = 6(x - 2)(x + 1)\)
\(f\) is strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\), i.e. where \((x - 2)(x + 1) < 0\).
The product of the two factors is negative exactly when \(x\) lies between the roots \(-1\) and \(2\):
For \(-1 < x < 2\): \((x + 1) > 0\) and \((x - 2) < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) product negative.
Outside \([-1, 2]\) both factors have the same sign, so the product is positive.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly decreasing for \(x \in (-1, 2)\).

\(f(x) = x + \dfrac{25}{x}\)  (domain: \(x \neq 0\))
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 1 - \dfrac{25}{x^2} = \dfrac{x^2 - 25}{x^2} = \dfrac{(x - 5)(x + 5)}{x^2}\)
\(f\) is strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\). Since \(x^2 > 0\) always, the sign of \(f'(x)\) is the sign of \((x - 5)(x + 5)\).
\((x - 5)(x + 5) < 0\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(x^2 < 25\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(-5 < x < 5\).
But \(x = 0\) must be excluded, as \(f\) is not defined there.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly decreasing for \(x \in (-5, 0) \cup (0, 5)\), i.e. for \(-5 < x < 5\), \(x \neq 0\).

\(f(x) = x^3 - 9x^2 + 24x + 12\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 18x + 24 = 3(x^2 - 6x + 8) = 3(x - 2)(x - 4)\)
\(f\) is strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\), i.e. where \((x - 2)(x - 4) < 0\).
The product is negative exactly when \(x\) lies between the roots \(2\) and \(4\):
For \(2 < x < 4\): \((x - 2) > 0\) and \((x - 4) < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) product negative.
Outside \([2, 4]\) both factors have the same sign, so the product is positive.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly decreasing for \(x \in (2, 4)\).

\(f(x) = x^3 - 12x^2 - 144x + 13\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 24x - 144 = 3(x^2 - 8x - 48) = 3(x - 12)(x + 4)\)
The critical points are \(x = -4\) and \(x = 12\). Sign of \((x - 12)(x + 4)\):
For \(x < -4\): both factors negative \(\Rightarrow\) product positive \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(x) > 0\).
For \(-4 < x < 12\): \((x + 4) > 0\), \((x - 12) < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) product negative \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(x) < 0\).
For \(x > 12\): both factors positive \(\Rightarrow\) product positive \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(x) > 0\).
At the critical points themselves, \(f'(-4) = f'(12) = 0\). Because the question says simply "increasing" / "decreasing" (not "strictly"), and because \(f'\) vanishes only at these two isolated points, the endpoints are included in each interval.
(a) \(f\) is increasing where \(f'(x) \geq 0\):
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is increasing for \(x \in (-\infty, -4] \cup [12, \infty)\), i.e. \(x \leq -4\) or \(x \geq 12\).
(b) \(f\) is decreasing where \(f'(x) \leq 0\):
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is decreasing for \(x \in [-4, 12]\).

\(f(x) = 2x^3 - 15x^2 - 144x - 7\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 6x^2 - 30x - 144 = 6(x^2 - 5x - 24) = 6(x - 8)(x + 3)\)
The critical points are \(x = -3\) and \(x = 8\). Sign of \((x - 8)(x + 3)\):
For \(x < -3\): both factors negative \(\Rightarrow\) product positive \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(x) > 0\).
For \(-3 < x < 8\): \((x + 3) > 0\), \((x - 8) < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) product negative \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(x) < 0\).
For \(x > 8\): both factors positive \(\Rightarrow\) product positive \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(x) > 0\).
(a) \(f\) is strictly increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\):
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly increasing for \(x \in (-\infty, -3) \cup (8, \infty)\), i.e. \(x < -3\) or \(x > 8\).
(b) \(f\) is strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\):
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly decreasing for \(x \in (-3, 8)\).

\(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1}\)  (defined for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), since \(x^2 + 1 > 0\))
Differentiate by the quotient rule:
\(f'(x) = \dfrac{(x^2 + 1)\cdot 1 - x \cdot 2x}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \dfrac{x^2 + 1 - 2x^2}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \dfrac{1 - x^2}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\)
The denominator \((x^2 + 1)^2 > 0\) always, so the sign of \(f'(x)\) is the sign of \(1 - x^2 = (1 - x)(1 + x)\).
(a) Strictly increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\):
\(1 - x^2 > 0\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(x^2 < 1\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(-1 < x < 1\).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly increasing for \(x \in (-1, 1)\).
(b) Strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\):
\(1 - x^2 < 0\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(x^2 > 1\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(x < -1\) or \(x > 1\).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is strictly decreasing for \(x \in (-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty)\).

\(f(x) = 3x + \dfrac{1}{3x}\)  (defined for \(x \neq 0\))
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 3 - \dfrac{1}{3x^2} = \dfrac{9x^2 - 1}{3x^2} = \dfrac{(3x - 1)(3x + 1)}{3x^2}\)
Since \(3x^2 > 0\) for \(x \neq 0\), the sign of \(f'(x)\) is the sign of \((3x - 1)(3x + 1)\).
Part 1 — on \(\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, 1\right)\):
Here \(x > \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(3x > 1\) \(\Rightarrow\) \((3x - 1) > 0\), and also \((3x + 1) > 0\).
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) on \(\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, 1\right)\), so \(f\) is increasing there.
(Check: at \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(f'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 3 - \dfrac{1}{3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)} = 3 - \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{5}{3} > 0\).)
Part 2 — on \(\left(\dfrac{1}{9}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\):
Here \(0 < x < \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(0 < 3x < 1\) \(\Rightarrow\) \((3x - 1) < 0\), while \((3x + 1) > 0\).
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) < 0\) on \(\left(\dfrac{1}{9}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\), so \(f\) is decreasing there.
(Check: at \(x = \dfrac{1}{5}\), \(f'\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right) = 3 - \dfrac{1}{3\left(\dfrac{1}{25}\right)} = 3 - \dfrac{25}{3} = -\dfrac{16}{3} < 0\).)
Hence \(f\) is increasing in \(\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, 1\right)\) and decreasing in \(\left(\dfrac{1}{9}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\).

\(f(x) = x - \cos x\)
Differentiate:
\(f'(x) = 1 - (-\sin x) = 1 + \sin x\)
For every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(-1 \le \sin x \le 1\).
Adding \(1\) throughout: \(0 \le 1 + \sin x \le 2\).
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) = 1 + \sin x \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).
Moreover \(f'(x) = 0\) only when \(\sin x = -1\), i.e. only at the isolated points \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\); between any two such points \(f'(x) > 0\).
Since \(f'(x) \ge 0\) everywhere and vanishes only at isolated points, \(f\) never turns.
\(\therefore\) \(f(x) = x - \cos x\) is increasing for all \(x\).

\(y = 5x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x\)
Step 1 — critical points:
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 15x^2 + 4x - 3 = (5x + 3)(3x - 1)\)
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = -\dfrac{3}{5}\) or \(x = \dfrac{1}{3}\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 30x + 4\)
At \(x = -\dfrac{3}{5}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 30\left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right) + 4 = -18 + 4 = -14 < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
At \(x = \dfrac{1}{3}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 30\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14 > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — the extreme values:
At \(x = -\dfrac{3}{5}\): \(y = 5\left(-\dfrac{27}{125}\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{9}{25}\right) - 3\left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = -\dfrac{27}{25} + \dfrac{18}{25} + \dfrac{45}{25} = \dfrac{36}{25}\)
At \(x = \dfrac{1}{3}\): \(y = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{27}\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right) - 3\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{5}{27} + \dfrac{6}{27} - \dfrac{27}{27} = -\dfrac{16}{27}\)
\(\therefore\) Maximum value \(= \dfrac{36}{25}\) at \(x = -\dfrac{3}{5}\); minimum value \(= -\dfrac{16}{27}\) at \(x = \dfrac{1}{3}\).
(These are the local maximum and local minimum. Being a cubic, \(y \to \infty\) as \(x \to \infty\) and \(y \to -\infty\) as \(x \to -\infty\), so there is no absolute maximum or minimum.)

\(f(x) = 2x^3 - 21x^2 + 36x - 20\)
Step 1 — critical points:
\(f'(x) = 6x^2 - 42x + 36 = 6(x^2 - 7x + 6) = 6(x - 1)(x - 6)\)
\(f'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 1\) or \(x = 6\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(f''(x) = 12x - 42\)
At \(x = 1\): \(f''(1) = 12 - 42 = -30 < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
At \(x = 6\): \(f''(6) = 72 - 42 = 30 > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — the extreme values:
\(f(1) = 2 - 21 + 36 - 20 = -3\)
\(f(6) = 2(216) - 21(36) + 36(6) - 20 = 432 - 756 + 216 - 20 = -128\)
\(\therefore\) Maximum value \(= -3\) at \(x = 1\); minimum value \(= -128\) at \(x = 6\).
(These are the local extrema; being a cubic, \(f\) is unbounded both ways, so there is no absolute maximum or minimum.)

\(f(x) = x^3 - 9x^2 + 24x\)
Step 1 — critical points:
\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 18x + 24 = 3(x^2 - 6x + 8) = 3(x - 2)(x - 4)\)
\(f'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 2\) or \(x = 4\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(f''(x) = 6x - 18\)
At \(x = 2\): \(f''(2) = 12 - 18 = -6 < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
At \(x = 4\): \(f''(4) = 24 - 18 = 6 > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — the extreme values:
\(f(2) = 8 - 36 + 48 = 20\)
\(f(4) = 64 - 144 + 96 = 16\)
\(\therefore\) Maximum value \(= 20\) at \(x = 2\); minimum value \(= 16\) at \(x = 4\).
(These are the local extrema; being a cubic, \(f\) is unbounded both ways, so there is no absolute maximum or minimum. Note the local maximum value \(20\) exceeds the local minimum value \(16\), as it must here.)

\(f(x) = x^2 + \dfrac{16}{x^2}\)  (domain: \(x \neq 0\))
Step 1 — critical points:
\(f'(x) = 2x - \dfrac{32}{x^3} = \dfrac{2x^4 - 32}{x^3} = \dfrac{2(x^4 - 16)}{x^3}\)
\(f'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x^4 = 16\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x^2 = 4\) (since \(x^2 = -4\) is impossible for real \(x\)) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 2\) or \(x = -2\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(f''(x) = 2 + \dfrac{96}{x^4}\)
At \(x = 2\): \(f''(2) = 2 + \dfrac{96}{16} = 2 + 6 = 8 > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
At \(x = -2\): \(f''(-2) = 2 + \dfrac{96}{16} = 8 > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — the extreme values:
\(f(2) = 4 + \dfrac{16}{4} = 4 + 4 = 8\), and \(f(-2) = 4 + \dfrac{16}{4} = 8\).
\(\therefore\) Minimum value \(= 8\), attained at both \(x = 2\) and \(x = -2\).
There is no maximum: as \(x \to 0\), \(\dfrac{16}{x^2} \to \infty\), and as \(x \to \pm\infty\), \(x^2 \to \infty\); so \(f(x) \to \infty\) and \(f\) is unbounded above.

\(f(x) = x \log x\)  (domain: \(x > 0\), since \(\log x\) requires \(x > 0\))
Step 1 — critical points (product rule):
\(f'(x) = 1 \cdot \log x + x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} = \log x + 1\)
\(f'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\log x = -1\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = e^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{e}\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(f''(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}\)
At \(x = \dfrac{1}{e}\): \(f''\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) = e > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — the extreme value:
\(f\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) = \dfrac{1}{e} \cdot \log\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) = \dfrac{1}{e} \cdot (-1) = -\dfrac{1}{e}\)
\(\therefore\) Minimum value \(= -\dfrac{1}{e}\) at \(x = \dfrac{1}{e}\).
There is no maximum: as \(x \to \infty\), \(x\log x \to \infty\), so \(f\) is unbounded above.

\(f(x) = \dfrac{\log x}{x}\)  (domain: \(x > 0\))
Step 1 — critical points (quotient rule):
\(f'(x) = \dfrac{x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} - \log x \cdot 1}{x^2} = \dfrac{1 - \log x}{x^2}\)
\(f'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\log x = 1\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = e\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(f''(x) = \dfrac{x^2\left(-\dfrac{1}{x}\right) - (1 - \log x)(2x)}{x^4} = \dfrac{-x - 2x + 2x\log x}{x^4} = \dfrac{2\log x - 3}{x^3}\)
At \(x = e\): \(f''(e) = \dfrac{2(1) - 3}{e^3} = -\dfrac{1}{e^3} < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
Step 3 — the extreme value:
\(f(e) = \dfrac{\log e}{e} = \dfrac{1}{e}\)
\(\therefore\) Maximum value \(= \dfrac{1}{e}\) at \(x = e\).
There is no minimum: as \(x \to 0^{+}\), \(\log x \to -\infty\) while \(x \to 0^{+}\), so \(\dfrac{\log x}{x} \to -\infty\) and \(f\) is unbounded below.

Let the two parts be \(x\) and \(30 - x\), where \(0 < x < 30\).
Objective — maximise the product:
\(P(x) = x(30 - x) = 30x - x^2\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(P'(x) = 30 - 2x\)
\(P'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(2x = 30\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 15\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(P''(x) = -2 < 0\) for every \(x\), so \(x = 15\) gives a maximum.
Step 3 — check the domain: at the endpoints \(x \to 0\) and \(x \to 30\) the product \(P \to 0\), so the interior critical point is indeed where \(P\) is greatest.
Step 4 — the answer:
The parts are \(x = 15\) and \(30 - x = 15\), and the maximum product is \(15 \times 15 = 225\).
\(\therefore\) The number \(30\) should be divided as \(15\) and \(15\); the maximum product is \(225\).

Let the two parts be \(x\) and \(20 - x\), where \(0 < x < 20\).
Objective — minimise the sum of their squares:
\(S(x) = x^2 + (20 - x)^2\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(S'(x) = 2x + 2(20 - x)(-1) = 2x - 40 + 2x = 4x - 40\)
\(S'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(4x = 40\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 10\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(S''(x) = 4 > 0\) for every \(x\), so \(x = 10\) gives a minimum.
Step 3 — check the domain: at the endpoints \(x \to 0\) and \(x \to 20\), \(S \to 400\), which is larger than the value at \(x = 10\); so the interior critical point is indeed where \(S\) is least.
Step 4 — the answer:
The parts are \(x = 10\) and \(20 - x = 10\), and the minimum sum of squares is \(10^2 + 10^2 = 200\).
\(\therefore\) The number \(20\) should be divided as \(10\) and \(10\); the minimum sum of the squares is \(200\).

Let the length and the breadth of the rectangle be \(x\) m and \(y\) m.
Constraint — the wire forms the perimeter:
\(2(x + y) = 36\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x + y = 18\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(y = 18 - x\), where \(0 < x < 18\).
Objective — maximise the area:
\(A(x) = xy = x(18 - x) = 18x - x^2\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(A'(x) = 18 - 2x\)
\(A'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(2x = 18\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 9\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(A''(x) = -2 < 0\), so \(x = 9\) gives a maximum.
Step 3 — check the domain: at the endpoints \(x \to 0\) and \(x \to 18\), \(A \to 0\), so the interior critical point is indeed the maximum.
Step 4 — the answer:
\(x = 9\) m and \(y = 18 - 9 = 9\) m; maximum area \(= 9 \times 9 = 81\) sq. m.
\(\therefore\) The dimensions are \(9\) m \(\times\) \(9\) m (the rectangle is a square), giving the maximum area \(81\) sq. m.

\(h = 3 + 14t - 5t^2\), where \(t \ge 0\) is the time.
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{dh}{dt} = 14 - 10t\)
\(\dfrac{dh}{dt} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(10t = 14\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(t = \dfrac{7}{5} = 1.4\)
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2h}{dt^2} = -10 < 0\), so \(t = 1.4\) gives a maximum.
Step 3 — the maximum height:
\(h = 3 + 14(1.4) - 5(1.4)^2 = 3 + 19.6 - 5(1.96) = 3 + 19.6 - 9.8 = 12.8\)
Step 4 — check the domain: at \(t = 0\), \(h = 3\); the ball rises up to \(t = 1.4\) and falls thereafter. So \(t = 1.4\) is where the height is greatest.
\(\therefore\) The maximum height the ball can reach is \(12.8\) units, attained at \(t = 1.4\).
(Equivalently, by completing the square: \(h = 3 + 14t - 5t^2 = \dfrac{64}{5} - 5\left(t - \dfrac{7}{5}\right)^2 \le \dfrac{64}{5} = 12.8\).)
diagramNote: Sketch the downward parabola of h against t, marking the vertex at (1.4, 12.8) and the starting height h = 3 at t = 0.

solution:
Place the semicircle \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\), \(y \ge 0\), with its diameter along the X-axis and its centre at the origin.
By symmetry, let the rectangle have its two vertices \((\pm x, 0)\) on the diameter and the other two, \((\pm x, y)\), on the arc, with \(0 < x < 1\).
So the rectangle has base \(= 2x\) and height \(= y\), where \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}\).
Objective — maximise the area:
\(A = 2xy = 2x\sqrt{1 - x^2}\)
It is easier to maximise \(A^2\) (valid, since \(A > 0\) means \(A\) and \(A^2\) are maximised together):
\(A^2 = 4x^2(1 - x^2) = 4x^2 - 4x^4\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{d(A^2)}{dx} = 8x - 16x^3 = 8x(1 - 2x^2)\)
\(\dfrac{d(A^2)}{dx} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 0\) (rejected — it gives no rectangle) or \(1 - 2x^2 = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) (taking \(x > 0\)).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2(A^2)}{dx^2} = 8 - 48x^2\); at \(x^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\): \(8 - 24 = -16 < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
Step 3 — check the domain: as \(x \to 0\) and as \(x \to 1\), \(A \to 0\), so the interior critical point is indeed the maximum.
Step 4 — the dimensions:
\(y = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), and base \(= 2x = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\).
Maximum area \(= 2xy = \sqrt{2} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 1\).
\(\therefore\) The largest rectangle has base \(\sqrt{2}\) units and height \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) units, and its maximum area is \(1\) sq. unit.
diagramNote: Draw the unit semicircle standing on the X-axis with the inscribed rectangle: base from (-x, 0) to (x, 0) along the diameter, upper vertices (-x, y) and (x, y) on the arc, and the radius to (x, y) labelled 1.

solution:
Let the base radius be \(r\) cm and the height be \(h\) cm. The tank is open at the top.
Constraint — the volume:
\(\pi r^2 h = \pi a^3\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(h = \dfrac{a^3}{r^2}\)
Objective — minimise the sheet used \(=\) (circular base) \(+\) (curved surface):
\(S = \pi r^2 + 2\pi r h = \pi r^2 + 2\pi r \cdot \dfrac{a^3}{r^2} = \pi r^2 + \dfrac{2\pi a^3}{r}\), \(r > 0\).
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{dS}{dr} = 2\pi r - \dfrac{2\pi a^3}{r^2}\)
\(\dfrac{dS}{dr} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(2\pi r = \dfrac{2\pi a^3}{r^2}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(r^3 = a^3\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(r = a\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2S}{dr^2} = 2\pi + \dfrac{4\pi a^3}{r^3}\); at \(r = a\): \(2\pi + 4\pi = 6\pi > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — check the domain: as \(r \to 0^{+}\), \(\dfrac{2\pi a^3}{r} \to \infty\); as \(r \to \infty\), \(\pi r^2 \to \infty\). So \(S\) is least at the only critical point, \(r = a\).
Step 4 — the dimensions:
\(h = \dfrac{a^3}{r^2} = \dfrac{a^3}{a^2} = a\)
So \(r = a\) and \(h = a\): the radius equals the height.
Minimum sheet \(= \pi a^2 + \dfrac{2\pi a^3}{a} = \pi a^2 + 2\pi a^2 = 3\pi a^2\) sq. cm.
\(\therefore\) The sheet required is minimum when the radius \(= a\) cm and the height \(= a\) cm (the minimum sheet then being \(3\pi a^2\) sq. cm).
diagramNote: Draw an open-top cylinder (no lid) with base radius r and height h labelled, indicating that the sheet = base circle + curved surface only.

solution:
The perimeter is \(10\) cm and one side is \(4\) cm, so the other two sides add up to \(10 - 4 = 6\) cm.
Let the other two sides be \(x\) cm and \((6 - x)\) cm.
Domain — the triangle inequality must hold for the sides \(4\), \(x\), \(6 - x\):
\(4 + x > 6 - x\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x > 1\); and \(4 + (6 - x) > x\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x < 5\). So \(1 < x < 5\).
Objective — maximise the area. Use Heron's formula with \(s = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5\):
\(A = \sqrt{s(s - 4)(s - x)\left(s - (6 - x)\right)} = \sqrt{5(5 - 4)(5 - x)(x - 1)} = \sqrt{5(5 - x)(x - 1)}\)
Maximise \(A^2\) (valid, since \(A > 0\)):
\(A^2 = 5(5 - x)(x - 1) = 5(-x^2 + 6x - 5) = -5x^2 + 30x - 25\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{d(A^2)}{dx} = -10x + 30\)
\(\dfrac{d(A^2)}{dx} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 3\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2(A^2)}{dx^2} = -10 < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
Step 3 — check the domain: at the endpoints \(x \to 1\) and \(x \to 5\), \(A^2 \to 0\) (a degenerate triangle), so \(x = 3\) is indeed the maximum.
Step 4 — the answer:
The other two sides are \(x = 3\) cm and \(6 - x = 3\) cm — an isosceles triangle with sides \(3, 3, 4\).
Maximum area \(= \sqrt{5(5 - 3)(3 - 1)} = \sqrt{5 \times 2 \times 2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\) sq. cm.
\(\therefore\) The other two sides are each \(3\) cm (the maximum area then being \(2\sqrt{5}\) sq. cm).
diagramNote: Draw a triangle with base 4 cm and the other two sides labelled x and 6 - x, noting the optimum is the isosceles triangle with sides 3, 3, 4.

solution:
Let the side of the square base be \(x\) cm and the height be \(h\) cm. The box is open at the top.
Constraint — the surface area \(=\) (square base) \(+\) (4 side walls):
\(x^2 + 4xh = 192\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(h = \dfrac{192 - x^2}{4x}\)
For \(h > 0\) we need \(0 < x < \sqrt{192}\).
Objective — maximise the volume:
\(V = x^2 h = x^2 \cdot \dfrac{192 - x^2}{4x} = \dfrac{x(192 - x^2)}{4} = 48x - \dfrac{x^3}{4}\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{dV}{dx} = 48 - \dfrac{3x^2}{4}\)
\(\dfrac{dV}{dx} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\dfrac{3x^2}{4} = 48\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x^2 = 64\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 8\) (taking \(x > 0\)).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{3x}{2}\); at \(x = 8\): \(-12 < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
Step 3 — check the domain: at \(x \to 0\) and at \(x \to \sqrt{192}\) (where \(h \to 0\)), \(V \to 0\); so the interior critical point is indeed the maximum.
Step 4 — the dimensions:
\(h = \dfrac{192 - 64}{4(8)} = \dfrac{128}{32} = 4\)
Largest volume \(= x^2 h = 64 \times 4 = 256\) cu. cm.
\(\therefore\) The box should have a square base of side \(8\) cm and height \(4\) cm, i.e. dimensions \(8\) cm \(\times\) \(8\) cm \(\times\) \(4\) cm, giving the largest volume \(256\) cu. cm.
diagramNote: Draw an open-top box with a square base of side x and height h, marking that the surface area counts the base plus four walls but no lid.

solution:
\(P(x) = (150 - x)x - 1625 = 150x - x^2 - 1625\), where \(x\) is the number of items sold per day.
Step 1 — critical point:
\(P'(x) = 150 - 2x\)
\(P'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(2x = 150\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 75\).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(P''(x) = -2 < 0\) for every \(x\), so \(x = 75\) gives a maximum.
Step 3 — the maximum profit:
\(P(75) = (150 - 75)(75) - 1625 = 75 \times 75 - 1625 = 5625 - 1625 = 4000\)
Step 4 — check the domain: \(P\) is a downward parabola in \(x\), so \(x = 75\) is where the profit is greatest for all \(x \ge 0\).
\(\therefore\) The firm should manufacture \(75\) items per day, and the maximum profit is \(4000\).

Let the two numbers be \(x\) and \(y\), with \(x + y = 15\), and let the quantity to be maximised be \(x^2 y^3\) (the square of one number multiplied by the cube of the other). Taking both numbers positive, \(y = 15 - x\) with \(0 < x < 15\).
Objective:
\(F(x) = x^2(15 - x)^3\)
Step 1 — critical points (product rule):
\(F'(x) = 2x(15 - x)^3 + x^2 \cdot 3(15 - x)^2(-1)\)
\(= x(15 - x)^2\left[2(15 - x) - 3x\right]\)
\(= x(15 - x)^2(30 - 5x)\)
\(= 5x(15 - x)^2(6 - x)\)
\(F'(x) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = 0\) or \(x = 15\) (both rejected — each makes \(F = 0\)) or \(x = 6\).
Step 2 — first derivative sign test at \(x = 6\):
For \(0 < x < 6\): \(x > 0\), \((15 - x)^2 > 0\), \((6 - x) > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(F'(x) > 0\).
For \(6 < x < 15\): \(x > 0\), \((15 - x)^2 > 0\), \((6 - x) < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(F'(x) < 0\).
\(F'\) changes from positive to negative at \(x = 6\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
Step 3 — check the domain: at the endpoints \(x \to 0\) and \(x \to 15\), \(F \to 0\); so \(x = 6\) is indeed the maximum.
Step 4 — the answer:
\(x = 6\), \(y = 15 - 6 = 9\), and the maximum value is \(6^2 \times 9^3 = 36 \times 729 = 26244\).
\(\therefore\) The two numbers are \(6\) and \(9\) (the number \(6\) being squared and the number \(9\) being cubed).

Let the rectangle have sides \(x\) and \(y\), and let its given (fixed) area be \(A\).
Constraint: \(xy = A\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(y = \dfrac{A}{x}\), with \(x > 0\).
Objective — minimise the perimeter:
\(P(x) = 2(x + y) = 2\left(x + \dfrac{A}{x}\right)\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 2\left(1 - \dfrac{A}{x^2}\right)\)
\(\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x^2 = A\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x = \sqrt{A}\) (taking \(x > 0\)).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2} = \dfrac{4A}{x^3}\); at \(x = \sqrt{A}\): \(\dfrac{4A}{A\sqrt{A}} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{A}} > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — check the domain: as \(x \to 0^{+}\), \(\dfrac{A}{x} \to \infty\), so \(P \to \infty\); as \(x \to \infty\), \(P \to \infty\). So \(P\) is least at the only critical point, \(x = \sqrt{A}\).
Step 4 — the conclusion:
At \(x = \sqrt{A}\): \(y = \dfrac{A}{\sqrt{A}} = \sqrt{A} = x\).
Since the two adjacent sides are equal, the rectangle is a square (of side \(\sqrt{A}\)), and the least perimeter is \(4\sqrt{A}\).
\(\therefore\) Among all rectangles of a given area, the square has the least perimeter.

Let the closed right circular cylinder have base radius \(r\) and height \(h\), and let its volume \(V\) be given (fixed).
Constraint: \(V = \pi r^2 h\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(h = \dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}\)
Objective — minimise the total surface area \(=\) (two circular ends) \(+\) (curved surface):
\(S = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r \cdot \dfrac{V}{\pi r^2} = 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{2V}{r}\), \(r > 0\).
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{dS}{dr} = 4\pi r - \dfrac{2V}{r^2}\)
\(\dfrac{dS}{dr} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(4\pi r = \dfrac{2V}{r^2}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(4\pi r^3 = 2V\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(V = 2\pi r^3\)
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2S}{dr^2} = 4\pi + \dfrac{4V}{r^3}\), which is \(> 0\) for \(r > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) minimum.
Step 3 — check the domain: as \(r \to 0^{+}\), \(\dfrac{2V}{r} \to \infty\); as \(r \to \infty\), \(2\pi r^2 \to \infty\). So \(S\) is least at this single critical point.
Step 4 — the conclusion:
Substituting \(V = 2\pi r^3\) into \(h = \dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}\):
\(h = \dfrac{2\pi r^3}{\pi r^2} = 2r\)
and \(2r\) is exactly the diameter of the base.
\(\therefore\) For a closed right circular cylinder of given volume and least surface area, the height is equal to its diameter.
diagramNote: Draw a closed cylinder with radius r and height h labelled, showing the optimum h = 2r, i.e. the height equals the base diameter.

solution:
Let the cylinder inscribed in the sphere of radius \(r\) have base radius \(x\) and height \(2y\), where \(y\) is its half-height measured from the centre of the sphere.
Constraint — a rim vertex of the cylinder lies on the sphere, so by Pythagoras' theorem:
\(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x^2 = r^2 - y^2\), with \(0 < y < r\).
Objective — maximise the volume:
\(V = \pi x^2 (2y) = 2\pi y (r^2 - y^2) = 2\pi (r^2 y - y^3)\)
Step 1 — critical point:
\(\dfrac{dV}{dy} = 2\pi (r^2 - 3y^2)\)
\(\dfrac{dV}{dy} = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(3y^2 = r^2\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(y = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}\) (taking \(y > 0\)).
Step 2 — second derivative test:
\(\dfrac{d^2V}{dy^2} = -12\pi y\); at \(y = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}\): \(-\dfrac{12\pi r}{\sqrt{3}} < 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) maximum.
Step 3 — check the domain: at the endpoints \(y \to 0\) (a flat disc) and \(y \to r\) (where \(x \to 0\)), \(V \to 0\); so the interior critical point is indeed the maximum.
Step 4 — the maximum volume:
\(x^2 = r^2 - \dfrac{r^2}{3} = \dfrac{2r^2}{3}\), and the height \(= 2y = \dfrac{2r}{\sqrt{3}}\).
\(V = \pi x^2 (2y) = \pi \cdot \dfrac{2r^2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{2r}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4\pi r^3}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}\,\pi r^3}{9}\)
\(\therefore\) The volume of the largest cylinder is \(\dfrac{4\pi r^3}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}\,\pi r^3}{9}\) cu. cm (attained when its base radius is \(\dfrac{r\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\) and its height is \(\dfrac{2r}{\sqrt{3}}\)).
diagramNote: Draw a vertical cross-section: a circle of radius r (the sphere) with an inscribed rectangle (the cylinder), marking the base radius x, the half-height y, and the right triangle giving x^2 + y^2 = r^2.

solution:
\(y = \log(1 + x) - \dfrac{2x}{2 + x}\), \(x > -1\)
Step 1 — differentiate. For the second term use the quotient rule:
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{2x}{2 + x}\right) = \dfrac{(2 + x)(2) - 2x(1)}{(2 + x)^2} = \dfrac{4 + 2x - 2x}{(2 + x)^2} = \dfrac{4}{(2 + x)^2}\)
\(\therefore\) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{1 + x} - \dfrac{4}{(2 + x)^2}\)
Step 2 — combine into a single fraction:
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(2 + x)^2 - 4(1 + x)}{(1 + x)(2 + x)^2} = \dfrac{4 + 4x + x^2 - 4 - 4x}{(1 + x)(2 + x)^2} = \dfrac{x^2}{(1 + x)(2 + x)^2}\)
Step 3 — determine the sign on the domain \(x > -1\):
Numerator: \(x^2 \ge 0\) always.
Denominator: \(x > -1\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(1 + x > 0\); also \(x > -1\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(2 + x > 1 > 0\), so \((2 + x)^2 > 0\).
\(\therefore\) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x^2}{(1 + x)(2 + x)^2} \ge 0\) for every \(x > -1\), and it equals \(0\) only at the single isolated point \(x = 0\).
Since \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} \ge 0\) throughout the domain and vanishes only at one isolated point, the graph never turns.
\(\therefore\) \(y = \log(1 + x) - \dfrac{2x}{2 + x}\) is an increasing function on its domain \((-1, \infty)\).

\(y = \dfrac{4\sin\theta}{2 + \cos\theta} - \theta\), \(\theta \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\)
Step 1 — differentiate. For the first term use the quotient rule:
\(\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{4\sin\theta}{2 + \cos\theta}\right) = \dfrac{(2 + \cos\theta)(4\cos\theta) - 4\sin\theta(-\sin\theta)}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2}\)
\(= \dfrac{8\cos\theta + 4\cos^2\theta + 4\sin^2\theta}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2} = \dfrac{8\cos\theta + 4\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\right)}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2} = \dfrac{8\cos\theta + 4}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2}\)
\(\therefore\) \(\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = \dfrac{8\cos\theta + 4}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2} - 1\)
Step 2 — combine into a single fraction:
\(\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = \dfrac{8\cos\theta + 4 - (2 + \cos\theta)^2}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2} = \dfrac{8\cos\theta + 4 - 4 - 4\cos\theta - \cos^2\theta}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2} = \dfrac{4\cos\theta - \cos^2\theta}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2}\)
\(= \dfrac{\cos\theta\,(4 - \cos\theta)}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2}\)
Step 3 — determine the sign on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\):
For \(\theta \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) we have \(0 \le \cos\theta \le 1\).
Hence \(\cos\theta \ge 0\); \(4 - \cos\theta \ge 3 > 0\); and \((2 + \cos\theta)^2 \ge 4 > 0\).
\(\therefore\) \(\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta\,(4 - \cos\theta)}{(2 + \cos\theta)^2} \ge 0\) for all \(\theta \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\); it is strictly positive on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and equals \(0\) only at the single endpoint \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (where \(\cos\theta = 0\)).
Since \(\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} \ge 0\) throughout and vanishes only at one isolated point, the graph never turns.
\(\therefore\) \(y = \dfrac{4\sin\theta}{2 + \cos\theta} - \theta\) is an increasing function of \(\theta\) on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
